subject: Engelska 6
title: Reading comprehension: opinion and argument
sourceSummary: Practise identifying the author's stance, distinguishing fact from opinion, and understanding counter-arguments as well as tone and bias in argumentative texts.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Social media has fundamentally reshaped how teenagers communicate, and not for the better. While it promises connection, study after study links heavy use to rising anxiety and shortened attention spans among young people. Parents and schools now have a responsibility to set clearer limits before another generation grows up struggling to concentrate or feel at ease offline."

What is the author's stance on social media use among teenagers?
questions.opener: Look at word choices like "not for the better" and "responsibility to set clearer limits" — what do they reveal?
choices: Neutral — the author simply reports research findings.
Critical — the author believes social media harms teenagers and limits are needed.
Supportive — the author believes social media improves communication.
Undecided — the author presents no clear opinion.
questions.explanation: Phrases like "not for the better" and the call to set "clearer limits" clearly show a critical stance towards social media use. The text is too judgemental to be neutral or undecided.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"The city council voted to ban plastic bags in all supermarkets starting next January. This is clearly the right decision, since plastic waste has become one of the biggest environmental problems of our time."

Which sentence in the text is a fact rather than an opinion?
questions.opener: A fact can be verified objectively — an opinion expresses a judgement.
choices: The city council voted to ban plastic bags in all supermarkets starting next January.
This is clearly the right decision.
Plastic waste has become one of the biggest environmental problems of our time.
Plastic bags should never have been allowed.
questions.explanation: That the council voted for a ban can be checked objectively — that is a fact. The other options contain judgemental words like "clearly the right" or "should never", which signal opinion.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Some argue that homework should be abolished because it adds unnecessary stress to students' lives. However, without any practice outside the classroom, many students would struggle to retain what they have learned, and teachers would lose an important tool for tracking progress."

What is the function of the word "However" in this text?
questions.opener: Words like "however" signal that the text changes direction — but towards what?
choices: It introduces an example that supports the first argument.
It introduces a counter-argument to the claim that homework should be abolished.
It signals that the author agrees homework should be abolished.
It has no particular function; it is decorative.
questions.explanation: "However" marks a turn: after mentioning the argument for abolishing homework, the text presents a counter-argument. This is exactly how counter-arguments are often introduced in argumentative text.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"The so-called 'experts' claim the new policy will save money, but anyone with common sense can see it will only burden ordinary families even more."

What does the phrase "so-called 'experts'" suggest about the writer's attitude?
questions.opener: Quotation marks and "so-called" around a word often signal irony or distrust.
choices: The writer fully trusts the experts' judgement.
The writer is being neutral and objective.
The writer is skeptical of and somewhat dismissive toward the experts.
The writer works as one of the experts.
questions.explanation: "So-called" and the quotation marks question the experts' authority — this signals distrust, not confidence. A neutral text would have written "experts" without these markers.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Electric cars produced 50% fewer emissions than petrol cars over their lifetime, according to a 2023 study. Even so, electric cars are obviously not a complete solution to climate change."

Which word in the second sentence signals that an opinion is being expressed?
questions.opener: Which word expresses a judgement rather than a neutral statement?
choices: Even so
climate
solution
obviously
questions.explanation: "Obviously" signals that the writer thinks something is self-evident — a judgemental word, not a neutral fact. The first sentence, which refers to a study, is instead a factual statement.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Proponents of the four-day work week point to happier, more productive employees. Critics counter that some industries simply cannot function with reduced hours. The truth, as with most reforms, probably lies somewhere between the two extremes."

How would you best describe the author's overall stance?
questions.opener: The last sentence often summarises the text's overall stance.
choices: Strongly in favour of the four-day work week
Strongly against the four-day work week
Balanced, acknowledging both sides without taking a strong side
Focused only on criticizing employers
questions.explanation: The text presents both sides fairly equally and ends by saying the truth "probably lies somewhere between the two extremes" — this shows a balanced, not a one-sided, stance.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and explain the author's stance on fast fashion, citing evidence from the text.

"Fast fashion retailers churn out new clothing lines every few weeks, encouraging shoppers to buy more than they need. Defenders of the industry point to the jobs it creates in manufacturing countries. Yet the environmental cost — from water pollution to textile waste in landfills — is difficult to ignore, and cheap prices often come at the expense of garment workers' wages and safety."
questions.opener: Weigh the arguments for and against each other — which side gets the most space and the strongest language?
questions.answer: The author is critical of the fast fashion industry, despite briefly acknowledging one argument in its favour.
steps: The text mentions an opposing point: "jobs it creates" — an argument FOR the industry.
But after "Yet" the text turns: environmental costs and poor working conditions are highlighted as more serious problems.
Word choices like "difficult to ignore" and "at the expense of" signal criticism, not neutrality.
Conclusion: the author acknowledges the counter-argument but clearly lands on a critical stance towards fast fashion.

questions.prompt: What should you look for to identify an author's stance and bias in an opinion text?
questions.opener: Five things to always scan the text for.
questions.answer: Loaded words (e.g. "so-called", "obviously", "sadly") reveal judgements · Turn words like "however", "yet", "but" mark counter-arguments or a shift in opinion · Facts can be verified objectively, opinions express judgement or interpretation · Who is quoted and how (named experts vs. "some say") can reveal bias · The concluding final sentence often reveals the text's main message or stance.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"The survey included 2,000 participants across five countries. The results were, frankly, disappointing."

Which sentence expresses an opinion?
questions.opener: The word "frankly" signals a personal judgement.
choices: The results were, frankly, disappointing.
The survey included 2,000 participants.
The survey included participants across five countries.
Neither sentence expresses an opinion.
questions.explanation: "The results were, frankly, disappointing" expresses the writer's personal disappointment — an opinion. The number of participants and countries, by contrast, are verifiable facts.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"Critics argue that remote work reduces collaboration. Yet many companies report that flexible schedules have actually boosted employee morale and output."

What is the function of "Yet" here?
questions.opener: "Yet" often marks a turn in the argument.
choices: It introduces a counter-argument to the criticism just mentioned.
It restates the criticism in different words.
It signals total agreement with the critics.
It has no logical function.
questions.explanation: "Yet" introduces a counter-argument to the criticism that remote work reduces collaboration, by highlighting the opposite experience reported by many companies.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"The billionaire generously 'donated' a fraction of his fortune to charity."

What does the use of quotation marks around "donated" suggest?
questions.opener: Quotation marks around a word often signal that the writer is questioning the word choice.
choices: The writer is skeptical about whether the act was genuinely generous.
The writer fully approves of the donation.
The word is being used in its normal, literal sense.
The writer made a spelling mistake.
questions.explanation: The quotation marks around "donated" suggest the writer doubts whether the act was genuinely generous, rather than simply stating a fact.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer.

"It is essential that we act now — every year of delay costs lives."

What does the word "essential" reveal about the author's stance?
choices: The author believes the action is urgently necessary, not merely optional.
The author is indifferent to the issue.
The author believes the action can wait.
The author is only stating a fact with no opinion.
questions.explanation: "Essential" signals that the writer sees the action as absolutely necessary, not merely desirable — this reveals a clear, urgent stance.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a fact rather than an opinion?
questions.opener: A fact can be measured and verified objectively.
choices: The average global temperature has risen by about 1.1°C since pre-industrial times.
This is the most important issue of our generation.
Everyone should be doing more to fight climate change.
It's shocking how little people care about the climate.
questions.explanation: The 1.1°C temperature rise is a measurable, verifiable figure. The other options contain judgemental words like "most important", "should", and "shocking".

questions.prompt: A writer states an opposing view before dismantling it with evidence. What is this technique typically called?
questions.opener: The technique means directly addressing an objection, not avoiding it.
choices: Addressing a counter-argument
Circular reasoning
A rhetorical question
An ad hominem attack
questions.explanation: Mentioning an opposing viewpoint and then countering it with evidence is called addressing a counter-argument, which strengthens the text's credibility.

questions.prompt: "Naturally, any reasonable person would agree with this proposal." What rhetorical technique does the word "naturally" employ here, and why is it potentially misleading?
questions.opener: The word "naturally" tries to turn an opinion into an obvious truth.
choices: It implies that disagreeing would be unreasonable, pressuring the reader to agree without providing evidence.
It objectively proves the proposal is correct.
It simply states a well-known scientific fact.
It has no persuasive effect at all.
questions.explanation: "Naturally" implies that anyone who disagrees is being unreasonable, which pressures the reader to agree without any actual evidence being presented — a rhetorical technique, not proof.
